items.prompt: A product-details endpoint gets 50 000 reads/s and about 10 writes/s; the database's p99 is 40 ms and the target is 10 ms.
items.why: Very read-heavy, the same items repeat, and the latency target is below what the DB can do → cache-aside in an in-memory store.

items.prompt: Users worldwide download the same product images and JavaScript bundles; latency from far regions is 300 ms.
items.why: Static, public content plus far-away users → cache it at the edge (CDN), close to the users rather than next to the app.

items.prompt: An event-logging service ingests 200 000 writes/s that are rarely read back; one database node can't keep up.
items.why: The bottleneck is write throughput and storage. A cache does nothing for writes, so split the data across nodes.

items.prompt: Analytics dashboards run heavy queries that slow down the primary database; results must be complete and may lag by a few seconds.
items.why: Arbitrary, non-repeating queries over complete data that may lag slightly → route them to read replicas. A key-value cache would rarely hit.

items.prompt: Every user's personalised home feed is computed by an expensive ranking job and then viewed many times over the next few minutes.
items.why: An expensive result that is reused and tolerates a few minutes of staleness → cache it per user. It's personalised, so it doesn't belong on a CDN.

items.prompt: One celebrity's profile key receives 30% of all traffic and the single cache node holding it is saturated.
items.why: The cache works; one key overloads one node. That's the hot-key problem: replicate or split that key, or add an in-process layer in front. Rebalancing the ring wouldn't split a single key.

items.prompt: Bank account balances must always show the latest committed value on every read.
items.why: Strong consistency on every read is an anti-signal for caching. Read from the primary (or synchronous replicas) instead of a cache that may be stale.
